Documentation → Tools & Studio → Transaction tracer

Transaction tracer

Send the same HTTP request through the appliance and directly to the backend, compare the two answers and their cookies, read the result as a HAR in the page, and see what the appliance is configured to change in between — the fastest way to tell "is it the WAF or the application?".

👤 ForViewerOperatorAdministrator
🔑 Permissionsmonitoring.probe_free monitoring.reveal_secrets
📍 WhereOperations → Troubleshooting → Transaction Tracer (every ADOM)

What is it?#

The transaction tracer answers the question every WAF incident starts with: is the appliance causing this, or the application? It sends one request through the appliance (leg A) and the same request straight to the backend (leg C), with the same Host header, and compares status, body and headers. A third view (leg B) lists what the appliance is configured to change on the way through — read from its server policy, never measured.

It is a page under Operations → Troubleshooting, in every ADOM. Until 2026-10-16 it was a window in the top-bar Tools menu.

What does it do?#

  • Leg A — through the appliance. A real request from the SATOM server to the address you give, measured phase by phase (TCP, TLS, time to first byte, total), with TLS version, cipher and certificate details.
  • Leg C — direct to the backend. The same method, path, headers and body, sent to the backend address but carrying leg A's Host header (and SNI), so both legs ask the same virtual host.
  • Diff and verdict. When both legs complete, one sentence tells you what the comparison means (see Result).
  • Leg B — derived. For a FortiWeb appliance and server policy you name, SATOM reads the policy, its pool, its web protection profile and its X-Forwarded-For rule and explains each setting that changes a request or response (monitor mode, TLS termination, client-real-IP, X-Forwarded-For, HSTS, Lua scripting, content routing, cache, health checks…). Fields the firmware does not carry are listed as not read, never as "off".
  • Cookies. Every cookie each leg sets, with its flags, the cookies the request sent, what a browser will do with each one, and — with both legs — which cookies the appliance issued, removed or rewrote (see Inspect cookies).
  • Reveal values. With monitoring.reveal_secrets, the real cookie, Authorization and API-key values, shown in the page and never written to the audit log (see Reveal cookie and credential values).
  • Exports. Copy curl gives one curl command per leg (using --resolve, so the Host/address pairing is kept); Download HAR saves satom-trace.har for browser developer tools. The HAR carries each leg's start time, server address, query string and cookies; credential values and the response body only when you ask for them (see View a HAR).
  • HAR viewer. View HAR shows the trace's HAR in the page as a table with a waterfall; Open a HAR file shows any HAR — one saved from browser developer tools included — read in your browser and never uploaded.
  • Correlate attack log. Lists attack-log entries on an appliance that fall within the trace window, as candidates (the attack log has one-second resolution and no request id, so nothing proves an entry is your request).

Redirects are never followed — the redirect is often the finding.

After a trace, a line under the legs shows the security-header grade of leg A's response — the HTTP Observatory scoring applied to the headers and cookies the trace already returned, with Open in HTTP Observatory. It makes no extra request and says it is partial: redirects, Subresource Integrity, CORS and certificate trust are graded only by a full Observatory scan of the site.

Requirements#

  • The SATOM server must be able to reach the appliance address and the backend over the network.
  • For Derive (leg B): a FortiWeb appliance that SATOM can read, and the exact server policy name.
  • For Correlate attack log: a completed trace and an appliance whose attack log SATOM can read.

Permissions#

Action Needs
Leg A to an appliance picked from the inventory list, with GET, HEAD or OPTIONS Any read permission (the coarse view key, granted for example by monitoring.view)
Leg A to a typed address, or any leg C (backend) <a class="dc-perm" href="permissions.html#monitoring-probe_free" title="Probe free targets — Point the certificate inspector and the transaction tracer at a
host SATOM does not manage. Inventory destinations never need this.">monitoring.probe_free
POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE <a class="dc-perm" href="permissions.html#monitoring-probe_free" title="Probe free targets — Point the certificate inspector and the transaction tracer at a
host SATOM does not manage. Inventory destinations never need this.">monitoring.probe_free and ticking the confirmation box for that request
Derive (leg B), Correlate attack log Any read permission; the appliance must be visible to you in the current ADOM
Reveal values, and a HAR with credential values and the response body monitoring.reveal_secrets (Administrator profile only; not in Operator)
View HAR, Open a HAR file, cookie flags and findings Any read permission

Users who hold users.manage are treated as holding monitoring.probe_free and monitoring.reveal_secrets (by design: they can grant themselves the keys). Without it, the free-target box for leg A is disabled with the placeholder free targets need the monitoring.probe_free permission, and the backend box is disabled with a backend is a free target: needs monitoring.probe_free.

❗Important

A backend (leg C) is always a free target, even when you type the address of a managed appliance. Users without monitoring.probe_free can therefore trace leg A from the inventory list only, and get no diff. The permission is checked only for the legs you actually fill in, so an inventory-only leg A trace works without it.

ℹ️Note

Changed in 2.11.0: a user without monitoring.probe_free can trace an inventory appliance (before, every trace was refused), a backend without a scheme is plain HTTP except on 443/8443, the inventory pick dials the appliance's registered management port, leg B lists only FortiWeb devices, and the tracer needs a read permission instead of sign-in alone.

How to use#

Trace a request#

  1. Open Operations → Troubleshooting → Transaction Tracer. A link can prefill the form: /txn-trace/?vip=…&backend=…&path=….
  2. Leg A — through the appliance: pick an appliance from the list, or leave — VIP typed on the right — selected and type a URL such as https://shop.example.com. List entries read <appliance> — management host:port: picking one sends leg A to that appliance's registered management address and port — not to one of its virtual servers. To trace a published site, type its VIP or URL.
  3. Leg C — backend (bypassing the appliance): type the backend address, for example backend.example:8080. Without a scheme, port 80 is assumed, and the backend is traced over HTTPS only on port 443 or 8443 and as plain HTTP on any other port. Write https:// to force TLS on another port.
  4. Choose the Method and Path (default /).
  5. Optional: Extra request headers (one per line), for example X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.9 or Cookie: SESSID=… to trace a signed-in request. Do not add Host — the tracer sets it.
  6. For a write method, fill Request body (mutating methods only) and tick I understand this sends a real write to that application from this server.
  7. Click Trace.

⚠️Warning

POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE are real requests to a live application, sent from inside your management network. Replaying a write "to see what happens" can create the very ticket you are investigating.

Inspect cookies#

After a trace, a Cookies — leg A / Cookies — leg C card lists every Set-Cookie of that response: Name, Value, Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Path, Domain and Expires / Max-Age. Sent with the request names the cookies your Cookie header carried. Value reads redacted unless the trace was run with Reveal values.

What a browser does with them explains each cookie's flags:

Badge Meaning
red The browser rejects or drops the cookie: SameSite=None without Secure, or a __Host- / __Secure- name that breaks its prefix rule
amber A risk to check: not Secure on an HTTPS response, not HttpOnly (correct for a CSRF-token cookie the page reads, wrong for a session cookie), or a Domain that is a bare name
grey Information: no SameSite, so browsers apply Lax

With both legs traced, Cookies A vs C says what the appliance did:

  • issued by the appliance (set on A, not on C) — its own session or persistence cookie;
  • set by the backend but not by the appliance — the appliance removed it;
  • rewritten — same name and path, different flags, shown backend → client (for example secure false → true).

A rewritten cookie on its own makes the verdict transforming.

Reveal cookie and credential values#

  1. Tick Reveal values under the request form. It is shown only to holders of monitoring.reveal_secrets; everyone else reads Cookie and credential values are redacted. Seeing them needs the permission monitoring.reveal_secrets.
  2. Click Trace. A yellow banner says the values are on screen; each one is marked revealed in the request headers, response headers and cookie tables.

The values exist only in the answer to your browser: the answer is not cached (Cache-Control: no-store), the audit log records revealed: true on txn_trace.run but never a value, and leaving or reloading the page discards them.

View a HAR#

  1. Run a trace, then click View HAR. The HAR viewer card lists one row per leg — Method, Status, URL, Type, Size, Time and a Waterfall bar. Type in Filter URL, status, method to narrow the rows.
  2. Click a row to see its request and response headers, query string, request and response cookies, timings and content.
  3. To include credential values and the response body, tick Include credential values and the response body in the HAR (audited) before View HAR or Download HAR (needs monitoring.reveal_secrets; the export is audited as txn_trace.har_values). Without it, cookie values are empty and the content holds only the body's SHA-256.

To read another HAR — for example one saved from the browser's developer tools while reproducing a problem — click Open a HAR file and pick it. The file is read in your browser and never sent to SATOM; files over 50 MB are refused. Content is always shown as text, never rendered as a page.

Read what the appliance forwards (leg B)#

  1. In Leg B and the attack log, pick the Appliance (FortiWeb). Only FortiWeb devices are listed, because leg B reads FortiWeb server policies.
  2. Type the Server policy name exactly as configured.
  3. Click Derive leg B. The card What <appliance> forwards for <policy> is labelled derived; pool members and a collapsible list of settings SATOM did not read follow it.

Find the matching attack-log entries#

  1. Run a trace first.
  2. Pick the appliance in Leg B and the attack log.
  3. Click Correlate attack log. Up to 20 candidate entries from the latest 60 attack-log rows are listed with the reason each was included.

Configuration#

Field Description Required Example
Leg A — through the appliance Inventory appliance (its management address and port), or host, host:port, [v6]:port, http(s):// URL Leg A or leg C https://shop.example.com
Leg C — backend Same formats; default port 80; without a scheme HTTPS only on 443/8443, plain HTTP otherwise Leg A or leg C backend.example:8080
Method GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE Yes GET
Path Request path and query (up to 2048 characters) Yes /checkout?step=2
Extra request headers Name: value, one per line, up to 24 headers No Accept-Language: es-MX
Request body Up to 64 KB; mutating methods only No {"id": 42}
Server policy (leg B) FortiWeb server policy name For Derive pol-shop

Response bodies are read up to 256 KB (each leg card shows the first 2,000 characters under Response body); each leg times out after 8 seconds.

Example#

🧪Example — The backend answers 200, the VIP answers 403

Leg A returns 403 Forbidden; leg C returns 200 OK. The verdict reads: The appliance answered 403 where the backend answered 200. THE APPLIANCE IS DECIDING this request — look at the attack log for this window before touching the application. Click Correlate attack log, then paste the matching entry into the False-positive explainer.

Result#

The verdict is one of four sentences:

Status Body Headers Verdict (shortened)
differ — — The appliance is deciding this request — check the attack log
same differ — Something is rewriting the response, or the legs did not reach the same application (content routing, another pool member, a cache)
same same differ The appliance is transforming, not blocking
same same same The appliance is not altering this transaction; a fault reproduced here is the application's

Header differences are grouped as Added by the appliance (present on A, absent on C), Present on C but not on A (the appliance removed it), Changed, and volatile headers (Date, ETag, Content-Length, request ids…) which are listed separately. Credentials (Authorization, Cookie, Set-Cookie, API-key headers) are shown as redacted with their length only, unless the trace was run with Reveal values; cookies are listed with their flags in the cookie cards.

Every trace is written to the audit log as txn_trace.run (targets, method, path, statuses, verdict, and revealed true or false); every Derive as txn_trace.derive; every HAR exported with values as txn_trace.har_values; every refusal for a missing permission as txn_trace.denied. No credential value is ever written to the audit log. See Audit log.

Troubleshooting#

"A free target requires the 'monitoring.probe_free' permission. Inventory destinations remain available."#

Possible causes - A request reached the server with a backend or a typed leg A address from a user without monitoring.probe_free (the panel disables both boxes for such users).

Solution 1. Trace leg A from the inventory list only, or 2. Ask an administrator for monitoring.probe_free.

"POST writes to the target application. It requires the 'monitoring.probe_free' permission."#

Possible causes - You chose a mutating method without the permission.

Solution 1. Use GET, HEAD or OPTIONS, or request the permission.

"POST is a real write to that application, issued from this server. Tick the confirmation to send it."#

Possible causes - The confirmation box was not ticked.

Solution 1. Tick I understand this sends a real write… and click Trace again.

"Give at least a VIP or a backend."#

Possible causes - Both leg A and leg C are empty.

Solution 1. Fill in at least one of the two.

"Only one leg was traced, so there is nothing to compare…"#

Possible causes - Only one of the two legs was given.

Solution 1. Give both a VIP and a backend to get the diff.

"Both legs must have completed. Leg A (via the appliance): TCP connect failed: …"#

Possible causes - A leg could not connect (TCP connect failed), failed the TLS handshake (TLS handshake failed) or the HTTP exchange (HTTP exchange failed).

Solution 1. Check that the SATOM node can reach that address and port. 2. A backend without a scheme is traced as plain HTTP except on 443/8443; give https://host:port for a TLS backend on another port, or http://host:443 for a plain one on 443.

"Revealing credential values requires the 'monitoring.reveal_secrets' permission. Trace without it: values stay redacted."#

Possible causes - A trace asked for values from an account without monitoring.reveal_secrets (the box is not shown to such accounts, so this comes from a stale page or a direct request). The refusal is audited.

Solution 1. Trace without Reveal values, or ask an administrator for the permission.

"A HAR with credential values requires the 'monitoring.reveal_secrets' permission."#

Possible causes - Include credential values… was sent by an account without the permission. SATOM refuses rather than returning a file with the values silently blanked, which would look complete.

Solution 1. Untick the box to get the redacted HAR.

"<file> is not JSON: …" or "Not a HAR file: there is no log.entries list."#

Possible causes - The file opened in the HAR viewer is not a HAR export (or is truncated).

Solution 1. Export again from the browser's developer tools (Save all as HAR) and open the new file.

"<file> is <n> MB; the viewer reads up to 50 MB."#

Possible causes - The HAR covers a long session.

Solution 1. Record a shorter session, or filter it in the browser's developer tools before saving.

"Pick an appliance and type a server policy."#

Possible causes - Derive leg B was clicked without both values.

"Could not read <policy> from <appliance>: …"#

Possible causes - The appliance is unreachable or the policy name is wrong.

Solution 1. Check the exact policy name on the Server policy page.

"Leg B is derived from FortiWeb server policies; <appliance> is a <kind>."#

Possible causes - A non-FortiWeb appliance was sent to Derive (the panel lists FortiWeb devices only, so this comes from a stale page or a direct request).

Solution 1. Reload the tracer page and pick a FortiWeb in Leg B and the attack log.

"Trace first, then pick the appliance whose attack log to search."#

Possible causes - Correlate attack log was clicked before a trace, or without an appliance in Leg B and the attack log.

"Attack log unavailable on <appliance>: …"#

Possible causes - SATOM could not read that appliance's attack log.

Advanced#

Advanced Why leg B is labelled "derived"

SATOM is not in the path between the appliance and the backend and cannot observe it. Leg B is built from configuration objects, and every row names the object and field it came from (for example policy.monitor-mode, xff.x-forwarded-for-support). A row such as LUA SCRIPTING IS ACTIVE on this policy means the rest of the table is a floor, not a complete account.

Advanced Correlation scoring

Entries are taken from the latest 60 attack-log rows. Rows whose timestamp falls within the trace window ±2 seconds are kept (rows without a parsable timestamp are kept for review only). A row scores higher when its source address matches the tracer's egress address — the local address each leg's connection left the SATOM server from, which is what the appliance logs as the client source. Up to 20 candidates are shown.

Advanced Destination policy

Targets are resolved once and the resolved address is dialled, with the hostname sent as Host/SNI. Every resolved address must pass: cloud-metadata, unspecified, multicast and reserved addresses are refused; ports 0, 22, 25, 465, 587, 6379 and 11211 are never dialled. TLS certificates are not validated by the tracer (inspection, not trust) — use the Certificate inspector to judge a chain.
